title: Predicting the next word
blurb: How a model writes by guessing one token at a time.

slides.title: A language model predicts what comes next
body: At its core, a language model does one job: given the text so far, predict the next token.
It adds that token to the text, then predicts again. Everything it writes — answers, emails, code — comes from repeating that one step.

visual.caption: One step of generation. The loop runs until the reply is finished.

items.label: Add it and repeat
items.text: “The cat sat on the mat” becomes the new input.

slides.title: Every possible token gets a score
body: The model doesn’t produce one answer. It gives a probability to every token in its vocabulary — likely ones get high scores, odd ones get tiny ones.
Those scores come from patterns in the huge amount of text it was trained on.

visual.caption: Probabilities made up for illustration. Real models score tens of thousands of tokens at every step.

items.heading: “mat” · 41%
items.text: A very common way to finish this sentence

items.heading: “moon” · 0.1%
items.text: Possible, but the model rates it very unlikely

slides.title: One token at a time, start to finish
body: A reply is built step by step, with each new token added before the next one is predicted. That’s why chat replies often appear a word or so at a time.
The model doesn’t plan a whole answer and then type it out. Once a token is written, everything after it builds on it — including any mistakes.

visual.caption: Each step feeds everything written so far back in as input.

slides.title: Predicting isn’t the same as knowing
body: Because the model writes whatever is most likely to come next, it’s very good at sounding fluent and natural.
But “likely to come next” and “true” aren’t the same thing — which is why later lessons matter.

visual.caption: Next-token prediction explains both the strengths and the slip-ups.

items.heading: Fluent by design
items.text: It has learned how sentences usually flow, in many styles and languages.

items.heading: No built-in fact check
items.text: Nothing in the prediction step looks up whether a statement is true.

items.heading: Shaped by training
items.text: Further training teaches it to act like a helpful assistant, but it still writes by prediction.

quiz.question: What does a language model do at each step of writing a reply?
options: Predicts the next token from the text so far
Looks up the full answer in a database
Copies a sentence it memorised word for word
Picks a word completely at random
quiz.explanation: Each step predicts one next token from everything written so far. Repeating that step builds the whole reply.

quiz.question: Why do chatbot replies often appear a little at a time?
options: The model is generated one token at a time, and each is shown as it’s produced
The app adds a typing delay to seem human
The model writes the reply backwards
quiz.explanation: Replies are produced token by token, so many apps show each piece as soon as it’s ready.

quiz.question: Given “The capital of France is”, why does a model give “ Paris” a high probability?
options: It searches the web before answering
“Paris” is the only token in its vocabulary
That pattern appeared often in the text it was trained on
It was hard-coded by a programmer
quiz.explanation: The probabilities reflect patterns learned during training. Common, well-documented facts tend to get high scores — less common ones may not.
